# Arizona HOA & Condo Insurance in 2026

Arizona is among the most HOA-saturated states in the country, so what happens in the association-insurance market touches an unusually large share of Arizona homeowners. Even without a single headline catastrophe, premiums have climbed with reinsurance and rebuild costs. Here is what is moving Arizona association pricing in 2026 and what your board should check before renewal.

## Why Arizona premiums keep rising

Arizona has seen fewer catastrophic events than California or Florida, yet associations still face steady increases. The drivers are national rather than local: the cost of the reinsurance behind master policies, construction and rebuild inflation, and a rising count of water, monsoon-wind, and wildfire-interface claims. Large master-planned communities and condominium associations, which carry big insured values, feel each rate move the most.

## The valuation problem in a fast-growing state

Arizona building costs rose sharply during the growth boom, and master policies written on pre-run-up valuations are commonly underinsured today. If a total loss triggers a coinsurance penalty, the shortfall lands on the association and its owners. A current [replacement-cost analysis](/hoa-replacement-cost-analysis.html) is the single most valuable check for most Arizona boards.

## Monsoon, wind, and the wildfire interface

Monsoon microbursts, haboob-driven wind and blowing debris, hail, and wildfire near the metro edges all show up in Arizona underwriting. Watch for deductible and exclusion language that shifts these perils back onto the association — a [coverage-gap review](/coverage-gap-review.html) is the fastest way to find it.

## HOA-dense means board-liability exposure is real

With so many associations, disputes over elections, assessments, and rule enforcement are common — and those are exactly the claims a [directors & officers (D&O) policy](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html) answers. In a state this HOA-heavy, confirming D&O limits keep pace with exposure is not optional.

## What Arizona boards should do before renewal

Get a current replacement-cost appraisal, review deductibles and exclusions, and benchmark the [master policy](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html) and D&O across carriers rather than auto-renewing. Start early enough to actually compare options — the associations that shop consistently pay less than the ones that do not.

> California HOA and condo association insurance in 2026 — wildfire-driven carrier pullbacks, the FAIR Plan and DIC wraps, and master-policy premium spikes. What association boards should review before renewal.

# California HOA & Condo Insurance in 2026

California has one of the hardest association-insurance markets in the country. Years of severe wildfire losses pushed major carriers to pull back from new business, drove more communities onto the state FAIR Plan, and sent HOA and condo master-policy premiums sharply higher. Here is what changed, where the market stands in 2026, and what every California board should do before its next renewal.

## Why California association premiums jumped

Wildfire catastrophe losses reshaped the entire California property market. Since 2023 several of the largest carriers restricted or paused new homeowners and commercial-property business in wildfire-exposed areas, and the reinsurance that backs association master policies grew far more expensive. Communities in the wildland-urban interface — the foothills and canyon edges around most metros — felt it first, but the pullback rippled into pricing statewide. Fewer carriers competing for your program means higher premiums and, just as important, higher wind and fire deductibles.

## The FAIR Plan and the DIC "wrap"

As admitted carriers retreated, more associations landed on the California FAIR Plan, the state's insurer of last resort. The FAIR Plan is a backstop, not a deal: it provides basic fire coverage with real limits and gaps, so boards typically pair it with a separate [difference-in-conditions (DIC) policy](/coverage-gap-review.html) to rebuild full protection — liability, water, theft, and more. That combination is more expensive and has more moving parts, and it is easy to end up with a gap between the two policies. If your association is on a FAIR Plan plus wrap, confirm the two actually fit together.

## California's regulatory reset

Under the state's Sustainable Insurance Strategy, regulators now let carriers use forward-looking catastrophe models and reinsurance costs in their pricing in exchange for commitments to write more coverage in wildfire-distressed areas. The intent is to bring admitted carriers back over time. For a board, the practical takeaway is that the market is shifting month to month — a program that had only one option a year ago may have new options now, which is exactly why re-shopping before you renew matters more in California than almost anywhere else.

## The replacement-cost trap

Rebuild costs climbed sharply, but many California master policies still carry valuations set before that run-up — which leaves the association underinsured. If a total loss triggers a coinsurance penalty, the shortfall falls on the association and its owners. A current [replacement-cost analysis](/hoa-replacement-cost-analysis.html) is one of the highest-value things a California board can do before renewal, and it also strengthens your position with carriers.

## What California boards should do before renewal

Start at least 90 days out. Get a current replacement-cost appraisal, and document your wildfire mitigation — defensible space and home-hardening increasingly affect both eligibility and price. Then benchmark the full program — the [master policy](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html), the DIC wrap, and [directors & officers (D&O) coverage](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html) — across carriers, not just the premium number. In a market moving this fast, the board that shops has leverage the board that auto-renews does not.

# Colorado HOA & Condo Insurance in 2026

In Colorado it is hail — not only wildfire — pushing association premiums up the fastest. Front Range storms, a hard look at wildfire exposure after the Marshall Fire, and a brand-new state insurer of last resort have all reshaped what boards pay and what carriers will cover. Here is where the Colorado market stands in 2026 and what your board should do before renewal.

## Hail is the number-one driver of Colorado increases

Colorado reporting has been clear that hail, more than wildfire, drives the largest share of the state's homeowners and association premium increases. The Front Range is one of the costliest hail corridors in the country, and repeated roof losses have pushed carriers to raise premiums, raise roof and hail deductibles, and add cosmetic-damage exclusions. For associations with a lot of roof area, that combination is a direct hit to the budget.

## Wildfire and the wildland-urban interface

The 2021 Marshall Fire reset expectations that wildfire is an urban-edge risk in Colorado, not just a mountain one. Carriers now scrutinize wildland-urban-interface exposure closely when they underwrite association property, which affects both eligibility and price for communities near open space.

## Colorado's new insurer of last resort

Colorado stood up a FAIR Plan so property owners with no other options have a backstop. Like every FAIR Plan it is limited and basic by design — a safety net, not a bargain — so an association that ends up there should confirm a wrap policy closes the [coverage gaps](/coverage-gap-review.html) the FAIR Plan leaves open.

## Roof age, deductibles, and cosmetic exclusions

Hail-market underwriting turns on roof age and material. Watch for large percentage hail deductibles and cosmetic-damage exclusions that can leave the association holding repair costs after a storm. Reviewing your [deductible structure](/hoa-insurance-deductibles.html) line by line is one of the most useful things a Colorado board can do.

## What Colorado boards should do before renewal

Document roof age, recent replacements, and any impact-resistant upgrades — they can earn real credits. Get a current replacement-cost figure, model the hail deductible in dollars, and benchmark the [master policy](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html) and [D&O](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html) across carriers. Start early; hail-exposed programs are taking longer to place.

## HOA insurance review FAQ

### How is condo insurance different?

Condo associations split responsibility between the master policy and unit owners' HO-6 policies. Gaps between the two are a common and costly problem we review.

### What about the deductible?

Master-policy deductibles — especially percentage and water deductibles — can shift large costs to owners. We review how yours is structured.

## Coverage Gap FAQ

### What's a coverage gap?

It's where your policy limits, exclusions, or structure leave the association exposed — like underinsured buildings, thin liability limits, or missing D&O.

### How common are they?

Very. Most boards find at least one gap in the first review, simply because policies renewed without a fresh look.

# Florida HOA Insurance in Crisis: What Every Board Needs to Know Before Renewal

Florida HOA and condo association insurance has been through the hardest market in a generation. Carriers exited the state, premiums climbed to 181% above the national average, and boards in Miami, Tampa, and Palm Beach found themselves with fewer options and higher bills at every renewal. The 2021 Surfside collapse then accelerated a regulatory overhaul that added new compliance burdens on top of an already strained market. Here is what drove the crisis, where the Florida market stands heading into 2026, and what every board needs to do before their next renewal.

## What broke the Florida market

The Florida property insurance market had been under pressure for years before it fractured. Carrier losses from hurricanes Irma (2017), Michael (2018), and Ian (2022) combined with runaway assignment-of-benefits litigation drove more than a dozen Florida-based insurers into insolvency between 2017 and 2024. Demotech — the primary ratings agency for Florida carriers — withdrew financial stability ratings from multiple companies including FedNat, Avatar, Weston, Bankers Specialty, and Frontline, sending HOA and condo boards scrambling for replacement coverage mid-term. Each exit shrank the competitive market and pushed more associations toward Citizens Property Insurance, the state's insurer of last resort, which was never designed to carry this kind of load.

## Citizens Insurance and what it means for your association

Citizens became the default carrier for thousands of Florida HOA and condo associations as private carriers withdrew — but Citizens is not a long-term solution and the state is actively moving policies out. Citizens approved a 14.2% statewide condo rate increase in 2025, and by the end of that year had shed approximately 541,000 policies through its depopulation program, which transfers policies to private carriers whether policyholders opt in or not. The Office of Insurance Regulation approved nine carriers for additional depopulation cycles in 2026. If your association is currently with Citizens, a takeout notice is likely — and boards that have not benchmarked the private market will have no leverage when it arrives.

## How SB 4-D changed the compliance picture for every Florida condo

The 2022 passage of SB 4-D — triggered directly by the Surfside collapse — created structural inspection and reserve requirements that now directly affect how carriers underwrite Florida condo associations. Buildings three stories or taller must complete milestone structural inspections at 30 years of age (25 years for coastal buildings) and every 10 years thereafter. Associations must also complete a Structural Integrity Reserve Study (SIRS) every 10 years, and as of January 1, 2025, boards are legally prohibited from voting to waive or reduce reserve contributions for the nine SIRS structural components. Carriers are strictly enforcing compliance: Citizens cannot issue or renew policies for non-compliant associations, and most private carriers will not bind coverage without a current appraisal and inspection documentation already on file.

## Signs of stabilization — but boards are still overpaying

There are genuine signs the Florida market is turning. The December 2022 SB 2-A reforms targeted assignment-of-benefits abuse and litigation costs, and 17 new property and casualty insurers have been approved to write in Florida since those reforms passed. American Coastal reported a 16.6% year-over-year decline in average Florida commercial property premiums in Q1 2026 — the first material rate rollback since the crisis began. Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation reported the state averaged just 0.8% in rate increases over the prior two years compared to 20–35% nationally. But premiums still sit roughly 181% above the national average, and boards that are auto-renewing without shopping their program are paying crisis-era pricing in a market that has quietly reopened.

## What Florida HOA and condo boards should do before their next renewal

The biggest mistake a Florida board can make right now is treating this renewal like the last three. The market that forced associations into Citizens or onto whatever carrier would write them is not the same market in 2026 — new carriers are actively seeking Florida HOA business, and boards with clean loss histories and current compliance documentation have real negotiating leverage they have not had since 2019. Get your milestone inspection results and SIRS in order before approaching the market. Request updated replacement cost appraisals that reflect current construction costs, not pre-inflation valuations. Then benchmark your full program — not just premium, but D&O limits, deductible structure, and carrier financial stability — against what is actually available before your board signs another renewal.

# HOA Insurance Carrier Review: Comparing Markets, Pricing & Renewal Strategy

Not every carrier underwrites HOAs the same way. Appetite, pricing, and coverage structure vary widely, and a policy that renews on autopilot is rarely the most competitive option available to your community.

## Why carrier appetite matters

Some carriers specialize in condo and HOA risk; others price it conservatively because it isn't their focus. Matching your association to a carrier that wants the business usually means better pricing and better coverage terms.

## What we benchmark

We compare your current program against available markets on limits, deductible structure, replacement cost, D&O, and total premium — so your board can see how your renewal stacks up before signing.

## Building a renewal strategy

A good review isn't just this year's price. It's a strategy: how to position your community, what to fix before the next renewal, and how to avoid year-over-year premium creep.

# Why HOA Insurance Costs Are Rising — And What Boards Can Do

Association insurance premiums have climbed sharply in recent years. Understanding what's driving the increases helps your board respond with strategy instead of just absorbing another hike.

## What's driving the increases

Rising construction and replacement costs, more frequent severe-weather claims, and carriers pulling back from certain regions have all pushed HOA premiums up — even for communities with no claims of their own.

## What boards can control

Boards can't control the market, but they can control how their risk is presented: accurate valuations, documented maintenance, sensible deductible choices, and a clean submission to the right carriers all influence pricing.

## The cost of doing nothing

Auto-renewing without a review is how communities end up overpaying. A competitive benchmark, done before renewal, is the most reliable way to keep increases in check.

# HOA Insurance Coverage Gaps: What a Review Catches Before They Become a Crisis

One review call can save your association money — or catch a gap before it becomes a crisis. The most expensive problems in HOA and condo insurance are rarely the premium printed on the renewal notice. They are the coverage gaps a board never sees until a claim exposes them — and by then the only options are an unbudgeted special assessment or a fight with a carrier. Here are the gaps an independent insurance review is built to catch, and why they hide in plain sight until it is too late.

## Why coverage gaps stay hidden until a claim

Having insurance is not the same as being protected. A master policy can be in force, premiums paid, certificates issued — and still leave the association badly exposed, because the gap lives in the fine print, not the declarations page. Most boards renew their program on autopilot: the agent sends a renewal, the treasurer approves it, and the same limits, deductibles, and endorsements roll forward year after year while construction costs, reserve balances, and the building itself all change underneath them. An independent review reads the policy the way a claim adjuster will — looking for the places where the coverage and the real-world exposure no longer line up.

## 1. Replacement cost that hasn't kept up

The single most common gap is a building insured for less than it would actually cost to rebuild. Construction and material costs have risen sharply, but many master policies still carry valuations set years ago. The danger is the coinsurance clause: if your building is insured below the required percentage of its replacement value, the carrier can reduce *every* claim payment proportionally — not just total losses. A community that thinks it is fully covered can find a routine claim paid at 70 cents on the dollar. A current replacement-cost appraisal is the fix. [See how a replacement cost analysis works →](/hoa-replacement-cost-analysis.html)

## 2. Percentage deductibles on wind, hail, and named storms

Boards often read the flat "all other perils" deductible and miss the one that matters. Wind, hail, hurricane, and named-storm losses frequently carry a *percentage* deductible — 2%, 5%, sometimes more — calculated on the insured value of the building, not the claim. On a multimillion-dollar property, that is a six-figure number the association (or its owners through a loss assessment) must cover before coverage even begins. A review surfaces the real out-of-pocket exposure on each peril so the board can fund it or negotiate it down. [Understand HOA deductible structures →](/hoa-insurance-deductibles.html)

## 3. Water damage sublimits and exclusions

Water is the highest-frequency claim most associations face, and it is exactly where carriers have tightened. Slow leaks, sewer backup, and certain pipe failures are increasingly capped by sublimits or excluded outright, even on policies that look comprehensive. A board that assumes water damage is "covered" can discover the protection is a fraction of the loss. The review identifies the sublimits and exclusions before a burst pipe makes them a problem.

## 4. Ordinance or law (code-upgrade) coverage

When an older building is damaged, it must be rebuilt to *current* code — newer wiring, fire systems, accessibility, structural standards — which can cost far more than replacing what was there. Without ordinance-or-law coverage, the insurer pays only to restore the original structure and the association absorbs the upgrade cost. For any community more than a couple of decades old, this is one of the most expensive gaps a review catches.

## 5. Directors & officers (D&O) gaps

Board members make consequential decisions — on assessments, contracts, rules enforcement, and reserves — and they get sued for them. Many associations carry a D&O policy that is too thin, excludes defense costs, or omits non-monetary claims and breach-of-contract actions. The review checks that the limit, the definition of "insured," and the defense provisions actually protect the volunteers serving on your board. [Review board liability & D&O coverage →](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html)

## 6. Loss assessment and the HO-6 handoff

Every condo and townhome community has a seam where the master policy ends and the unit owner's HO-6 policy begins — defined by the governing documents as bare-walls, single-entity, or all-in. When the master policy's structure and the owners' policies are not aligned, a loss can fall into the gap between them, leaving owners underinsured and the association exposed to assessment. A review maps that boundary and confirms the loss-assessment coverage on both sides lines up with how the master policy is actually written.

## 7. Fidelity / crime coverage that hasn't scaled with reserves

Associations handle real money, and embezzlement by a manager, board member, or vendor is a genuine risk. Fidelity (crime) coverage protects those funds — but the limit needs to reflect the maximum dollars the association controls at any point, including growing reserve balances. As reserve studies push communities to hold more, a fidelity limit set years ago can leave a large share of the association's cash unprotected. The review right-sizes it.

## What an independent review actually does

A review is not a sales pitch and it does not disrupt your current coverage. We read your existing master policy, declaration pages, and renewal the way a carrier and a claims adjuster would, benchmark the full program — limits, deductible structure, endorsements, D&O, and carrier financial strength — against what is actually available in today's market, and hand the board a plain-language summary of where the gaps and the savings are. It is free, there is no obligation to switch, and no board vote is required to begin. It works for [condo associations](/condo-association-insurance.html), townhome communities, and master-planned [HOA master policies](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html) alike.

# HOA Insurance Deductibles: Wind, Hail, Water & Percentage Deductibles Explained

Deductibles are one of the most overlooked parts of an HOA master policy, and one of the most expensive to get wrong. The structure of your deductibles decides who pays — the association, the carrier, or individual owners — when a claim happens.

## Flat vs. percentage deductibles

A flat deductible is a fixed dollar amount per claim. A percentage deductible is a share of the insured value, which on a large building can be tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. Many associations don't realize a single storm could trigger a percentage deductible far larger than their reserves.

## Wind, hail, wildfire, and water

Carriers increasingly apply separate, higher deductibles for wind, hail, wildfire, and water damage in higher-risk regions. These peril-specific deductibles often hide the real out-of-pocket exposure your board would face in a claim.

## Who actually pays

When a master-policy deductible is high, the cost frequently lands on the association's budget — or gets passed to owners through a special assessment. Reviewing how your deductibles are structured is the first step to avoiding a surprise.

# HOA Internet & Cable Contracts: Bulk Agreements, Terms & Renewals

Bulk internet and cable agreements are some of the largest long-term contracts an association signs — and some of the least reviewed. The terms your board agrees to can lock the community in for years.

## How bulk agreements work

In a bulk agreement, the association contracts service for the whole community at a negotiated per-unit rate, usually folded into dues. Done well, it lowers costs; done poorly, it locks in rates and terms that don't age well.

## What to watch in the terms

Auto-renewal clauses, annual escalators, exclusivity, and equipment obligations all deserve scrutiny. These are where multi-year contracts quietly become expensive.

## Reviewing before you sign

Because these agreements run for years, a review before signing or renewing is worth far more than the time it takes. We help boards compare terms and negotiate from a stronger position.

# HOA Landscaping Contract Review: Scope, Pricing & Accountability

Landscaping is often one of an association's biggest recurring vendor expenses, and one of the most common sources of owner complaints. A clear, well-reviewed contract protects both the budget and the community's appearance.

## Define the scope

Vague scopes lead to disputes. A strong contract spells out mowing frequency, trimming, seasonal cleanups, irrigation responsibility, and what counts as extra work — so expectations are clear on both sides.

## Pricing and escalators

Multi-year landscaping contracts often include annual price escalators. Reviewing them — and benchmarking against the market — keeps the association from overpaying as the term runs on.

## Accountability and exit

Performance standards, response times, and reasonable termination rights give the board leverage if service slips. We help associations review these terms before signing.

# HOA Trash & Recycling Contract Review: Terms, Rates & Renewals

Waste and recycling service is a steady line item in nearly every association budget. Because the contracts are routine, they often renew without review — and the rates climb quietly year after year.

## What drives the rate

Pickup frequency, container counts, fuel and environmental surcharges, and contamination fees all affect what your community actually pays. Many associations are surprised by how much is in the surcharges.

## Auto-renewal and escalators

Trash contracts frequently include automatic renewals and annual rate increases. Without a review window, a board can miss the chance to renegotiate or shop the service.

## Reviewing for savings

Benchmarking your service and terms against the market — before the renewal date — is the simplest way to keep waste costs from drifting. We help boards do exactly that.

# HOA Vendor Contract Review: Protecting the Association in Every Agreement

Every vendor agreement an association signs carries risk as well as cost. A consistent review process protects the community's budget and shields the board from exposure buried in the fine print.

## Insurance and indemnification

Vendors working on association property should carry adequate insurance and name the HOA as additional insured. Indemnification language decides who's responsible when something goes wrong — it's worth getting right.

## Scope, pricing, and term

Clear scope, transparent pricing, and a sensible term protect the association from disputes and runaway costs. Multi-year terms and escalators especially deserve a second look.

## A consistent review process

Reviewing vendor contracts the same way every time — insurance, scope, pricing, termination — gives boards leverage and consistency. We help associations build that review into renewals.

# How HOA Cable & Bulk TV Agreements Work

Bulk cable and TV agreements can be a real amenity for a community — or a long-term cost that outlives its value. Understanding how they work helps your board decide whether yours still makes sense.

## The bulk model

The association contracts TV service for every unit at a discounted group rate, usually billed through dues. The trade-off is that every owner pays, whether they use the service or not.

## How they're priced

Pricing is driven by channel lineup, term length, take rate, and escalators. As streaming changes how owners watch, the value of a bulk TV agreement is worth re-evaluating at each renewal.

## What to review before renewing

Term length, auto-renewal, escalators, and equipment obligations are the key terms. A review before renewal keeps the association from locking into outdated service.

# Nevada HOA Insurance 2026: Las Vegas Master Policy & Rising Costs

> Nevada HOA and condo association insurance in 2026 — Las Vegas master-planned and high-rise communities face rising master-policy premiums. What boards should review before renewal.

**Nevada HOA and condo carriers are tightening fast — boards that wait get fewer options and higher bills at renewal.** Get a free, board-ready review from a **licensed broker** — before renewal.

**4,000+ communities served · $3B+ in coverage reviewed · 38 states · Licensed broker · Your info is never sold or shared.**

**Source:** https://hoacontracts.com/nevada-hoa-insurance · HOA Contracts · Free, no-obligation review · Call **(208) 361-4295**

---

# Nevada HOA & Condo Insurance in 2026

Nevada — and the Las Vegas valley in particular — is packed with master-planned and high-rise communities, and their master policies have climbed with reinsurance and rebuild costs. Nevada is not a coastal or wildfire-headline state, but the dollars are large because the insured values are large. Here is what is driving Nevada association pricing in 2026 and what your board should do before renewal.

## Why Nevada premiums are rising

Nevada association premiums are rising mostly on national pressures — the cost of reinsurance passed through to master policies, construction and rebuild inflation, and larger catastrophe loads across the industry. Because high-rise and large master-planned communities carry substantial insured values, even a modest rate increase becomes a big dollar figure at the association level.

## High-rise and master-planned communities

The Las Vegas and Henderson areas are full of high-rises and large HOAs with complex master programs spanning property, general liability, umbrella, and [D&O](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html). More value at risk means more underwriting scrutiny — and more room for a [condo or association program](/condo-association-insurance.html) to be mispriced or mismatched to the buildings it covers.

## Replacement cost and valuation

Rebuild costs are up across the Southwest, and Nevada master policies with stale valuations are commonly underinsured. A coinsurance penalty at a total loss falls on the association, so a current [replacement-cost analysis](/hoa-replacement-cost-analysis.html) is worth doing before you shop.

## Deductibles and coverage gaps

Wind, wildfire-interface, and water-damage claims all shape Nevada underwriting. Watch the deductible structure and exclusions that can shift cost back to the association and its owners — a [coverage-gap review](/coverage-gap-review.html) is the quickest way to surface them.

## What Nevada boards should do before renewal

Get a current appraisal, review your deductibles, and benchmark the [master policy](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html) and D&O across carriers. Start 60 to 90 days out, especially for high-rise programs, which take longer to place. Shopping the program is how Nevada boards keep a large insured value from turning into an oversized premium.

**Other state guides:** [California](/california-hoa-insurance.html) · [Texas](/texas-hoa-insurance.html) · [Colorado](/colorado-hoa-insurance.html) · [Arizona](/arizona-hoa-insurance.html) · [Florida](/florida-hoa-insurance-crisis.html)

# Texas HOA Insurance 2026: Wind, Hail & Master Policy Costs

> Texas HOA and condo association insurance in 2026 — wind and hail deductibles, premium spikes, and coastal windstorm exposure. What association boards should review before renewal.

**Texas HOA and condo carriers are tightening fast — boards that wait get fewer options and higher bills at renewal.** Get a free, board-ready review from a **licensed broker** — before renewal.

**4,000+ communities served · $3B+ in coverage reviewed · 38 states · Licensed broker · Your info is never sold or shared.**

**Source:** https://hoacontracts.com/texas-hoa-insurance · HOA Contracts · Free, no-obligation review · Call **(208) 361-4295**

---

# Texas HOA & Condo Insurance in 2026

Texas associations face some of the steepest property premiums in the country — hail across the north, windstorm on the coast, and one of the largest HOA footprints of any state. The pressure is real, but the detail that catches the most boards off guard is not the premium; it is the deductible. Here is what is driving Texas association pricing in 2026 and what your board should check before renewal.

## Hail and wind are driving Texas premiums

North and Central Texas sit in one of the most hail-battered corridors in the nation, and repeated severe storms have driven heavy carrier losses and steady rate increases for associations. On the Gulf Coast, named-storm and windstorm exposure adds a second layer. The result is a market where master-policy premiums have risen fast — and where carriers are managing their risk as much through deductible structure as through price.

## Watch your wind/hail deductible — it may be a percentage

This is the one every Texas board should check: many master policies carry a percentage wind/hail deductible — often 1% to 5% of the insured value — rather than a flat dollar amount. On a large community that can be a six-figure number the association has to absorb before coverage responds after a storm. Boards routinely discover this only when a claim lands. Read your [deductible structure](/hoa-insurance-deductibles.html) now, and make sure a [coverage-gap review](/coverage-gap-review.html) models it in real dollars against your buildings.

## Coastal associations and TWIA

In the designated coastal counties, standard wind coverage can be hard to place, and the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) serves as the fallback for wind and hail — with its own limits and requirements. Coastal boards often pair TWIA with additional layers to rebuild full protection, and the fit between those policies is exactly where gaps hide.

## Replacement cost in a high-inflation rebuild market

Texas construction costs rose sharply, and master policies with stale valuations are commonly underinsured. A coinsurance penalty at a total loss falls on the association and its owners, so a current [replacement-cost analysis](/hoa-replacement-cost-analysis.html) is worth doing before you approach the market — it protects the community and strengthens your submission.

## What Texas boards should do before renewal

Model your wind/hail deductible in dollars, not percentages. Get an updated appraisal. Then benchmark the [master policy](/hoa-master-insurance-policies.html) and [board D&O](/hoa-board-liability-insurance.html) across carriers, and start early — coastal and hail-exposed programs take longer to place. The goal is simple: no surprises in the deductible, and no premium you did not test against the market.

**Other state guides:** [California](/california-hoa-insurance.html) · [Colorado](/colorado-hoa-insurance.html) · [Arizona](/arizona-hoa-insurance.html) · [Nevada](/nevada-hoa-insurance.html) · [Florida](/florida-hoa-insurance-crisis.html)
